opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think Tesla is one of the most serious players in this space, and I have a lot of respect for what they've built. Their approach is quite distinctive: vision-only, end-to-end neural networks, and an enormous fleet collecting real-world data every day. In terms of data scale and the ability to iterate quickly, nobody else really comes close. Their FSD system has improved dramatically over the last couple of years, especially since they moved to the end-to-end architecture.

But I would separate two things: driver assistance and true robotaxi operation. Going from a system that works most of the time with a human supervising to one that runs without anyone behind the wheel is not a linear step. It's a qualitative leap. For a robotaxi, the long tail matters enormously. You need safety performance that is not just as good as a human driver, but significantly better, maybe ten times better, before regulators and the public will truly accept it at scale.

That's where I still have some reservations about a pure vision approach. Cameras are powerful, and with enough data and compute you can solve a great deal. But in extreme conditions like heavy rain, fog, glare, or night scenarios, having redundancy from lidar, radar, and high-precision maps gives you an extra margin of safety. Companies like Waymo, and in China Apollo Go, have taken that more conservative, multi-sensor route, and they've already accumulated many millions of fully driverless miles on public roads. That operational experience—dispatching, remote assistance, handling edge cases, working with cities—is also a big part of running a robotaxi business, not just the driving algorithm itself.

On the other hand, Tesla's big advantage is cost and scalability. If their approach works, they can deploy at a scale and price point that others would find very hard to match. Sensor costs are coming down for everyone, though, so that gap is narrowing.

So my overall assessment is: Tesla definitely has the potential, and I believe they will get there. But the timeline is likely to be longer than Elon's projections, as it often is. In the end, I think the industry will converge. The end-to-end, data-driven methods Tesla champions will be widely adopted, while some form of sensor redundancy will remain important for safety at L4. It's not really a question of whether robotaxis will happen, but how fast and who gets to large-scale, safe, and profitable operation first.

r001.rationale: It contrasts supervised FSD with driverless operation and says robotaxis need safety well beyond human performance for public acceptance, communicating the higher standard without a human available to take over.

r002.rationale: It links Tesla’s potential to deploy at scale to its large real-world data fleet, rapid iteration, and cost and scalability advantages.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think Tesla has some very real strengths, and some very real open questions. Let me take them one at a time.

The strengths first. Tesla has something no other player in this space has: a fleet of several million vehicles on the road, all equipped with cameras, all sending data back. That gives them a scale of real-world driving data that nobody else can match. And Elon's bet on an end-to-end, vision-only approach, where the neural network goes from pixels to steering and acceleration, is actually quite elegant. If you believe that scaling laws apply to driving the way they apply to language models, then more data and more compute should keep pushing the capability curve up. FSD has improved a lot over the past two years. Anyone who has ridden in version 12 or 13 can feel that.

The second strength is cost. Tesla builds its own cars, its own chips, its own software stack. A robotaxi is ultimately a business about cost per mile, and vertical integration matters enormously there.

Now the open questions. The gap between a very good driver-assist system and a true driverless system is not a small gap. It's actually the hardest part. With FSD, a human is still responsible, so the system can be 99.9 percent reliable and that's fine. For a robotaxi with no one in the car, you need something closer to 99.9999 percent. That last stretch is where the long tail lives, the rare and strange situations. Waymo took more than a decade and used lidar, radar, high-definition maps, and a lot of redundancy to get there, and they still operate in geofenced cities. Tesla is trying to get there with cameras alone and without maps. I don't think that's impossible, but it's a bet that hasn't been proven yet, and the burden of proof is high because safety is involved.

The second question is operations. Running a robotaxi service is not just an AI problem. It's remote assistance, fleet management, cleaning, charging logistics, regulators in every city, insurance, incident response. Waymo has learned a lot of painful lessons there. Tesla is early on that curve. What they have launched in Austin so far is still small and still has safety monitors involved.

So my overall assessment: in terms of technology trajectory and cost structure, Tesla may have the best long-term position of anyone. In terms of actual proven driverless operation today, Waymo is clearly ahead, and the Chinese players like Baidu's Apollo Go and Pony.ai have also accumulated real operating experience. The question is really about time. If Tesla's approach works, it could scale faster than anyone, because the cars are already out there. If it hits a ceiling, that ceiling might be hard to break through without adding sensors they've chosen not to use.

I'd put it this way: I take their potential seriously, but I'd want to see the data on unsupervised miles and intervention rates before I'd say they've arrived. In autonomous driving, we've all learned to be humble about timelines.

r001.rationale: It says a driverless robotaxi has no one in the car to take responsibility and needs much higher reliability than supervised FSD.

r002.rationale: It connects Tesla’s potential to scale faster to its existing fleet of millions of cars, driving data, and integrated vehicle and software capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think Tesla has significant potential, but I would distinguish between demonstrating autonomous driving and operating a reliable robotaxi service. A robotaxi has to handle situations where there is no driver available to take over. That is a much higher bar.

Tesla’s advantage is the integration of the vehicle, the software, and the data collected from its fleet. That gives it a strong foundation for improving the system and potentially bringing costs down. The key question is whether it can demonstrate sufficiently reliable performance across the conditions in which it intends to operate.

There is also an operational challenge: maintaining the fleet, assisting passengers, dealing with blocked roads, and working with regulators. So I see a real opportunity, but I would judge progress by safe, repeatable operation within a clearly defined service area, rather than by a promised launch date.

r001.rationale: It says a robotaxi must handle situations with no driver available to take over, setting a higher bar than demonstrating autonomous driving.

r002.rationale: It identifies Tesla’s vehicle, software, and fleet data as a strong foundation and mentions lowering costs, but does not clearly connect those foundations to operating robotaxis at larger scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I would separate the potential from the timing. Tesla has a promising foundation: a large vehicle fleet, integration between software and hardware, and experience manufacturing electric vehicles at scale. Those could become significant advantages in a robotaxi business.

But the key question is whether the vehicle can operate safely without a human driver within clearly defined conditions. That is a different standard from driver assistance. You also need reliable fleet operations, maintenance, insurance, and regulatory approval.

So I see substantial potential, but I would be cautious about predicting a timetable. I would look for demonstrated safety and dependable service in a limited area first, then evaluate whether that can expand economically.

r001.rationale: It says robotaxis must operate safely without a human driver and distinguishes that from driver assistance, which communicates the higher standard and lack of human takeover.

r002.rationale: It links Tesla’s robotaxi potential to its existing fleet, software–hardware integration, and scaled EV manufacturing, describing these as foundations that could support expansion.
